new_statements.quote: Half of the Grassfields languages (that is, the Mbam-Nkam group, to which the Ngemba, Limbum, Mfumte, Yamba and Mbaw belong) are fairly closely related to the Bantu languages that are spoken almost all over Africa south of the Equator. [p. 18-19] ... All Grassfields languages are tone languages, which means that — contrary to European languages for instance — the higher or lower pitch of the voice on each syllable affects the meaning of the words and the sentences. These tones form patterns. Similar tone patterns associated with similar meaning can be found in many related languages. [p. 33]

Both quoted passages are verbatim at the stated loca…
new_statements.relation_note: States that all Grassfields languages, a set in which it explicitly places Mbaw (Mbam-Nkam), are tone languages; no stress statement; no Mbaw forms.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mbaw is classed among the Mbam-Nkam Grassfields languages, and all Grassfields languages are said to be tone languages (pitch on each syllable distinguishes words and sentences); nothing about stress or accent.
new_statements.identity_note: 'Mbaw' is named as one of the Mbam-Nkam (Grassfields) languages alongside Ngemba, Limbum, Mfumte and Yamba, i.e. the Nkambe-group Mbaw = ALCAM 907 = Mbe'/Mbo' [mtk]; the book's 'N.E. Federation (Nkambe): Mbembe, Misaje, Tang, Mbaw, War, Mfumte, Wiya, Mbem' is the same Mbaw area. The book is a regional history by an anthropologist and a sociologist summarising the Grassfields Bantu Working Group / Hombert classification; it contains no data from Mbaw itself.

sources.citation: Watters, John R. 2003. Grassfields Bantu. In Nurse & Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 225-256. London: Routledge.
sources.note: Nothing about Mbe' stress. p. 231 lists '(e) Mbi' (a:Mbaw, Mbo).. no estimate. Refers to area known as Mbɔ Plain, on northern border of Yamba. Each of thirteen villages has its own language, some more closely related to Tikar. Same as Mbe' in Grimes (2000:44) (Ginny Bradley pc).' Section 2.4 Tones (p. 227) is a general statement that Grassfields Bantu languages are tonal (H/L, floating tones); it names other languages, never Mbe'.

sources.citation: Mafiamba, P. C. 1969. Notes on the polyglot populations of Nkambe. Abbia: revue culturelle camerounaise / Cameroon cultural review 21 (janv.-avril 1969): 59-90. (Section 1 'The Mbaw', pp. 59-63.)
sources.note: No phonology content at all: no sounds, tones, stress or wordlist. The linguistic content is limited to which language (Tikar, Mambila, Kaka = Mfumte/Mbem) each Mbaw Plain village speaks or understands, Tikar as lingua franca, population (3,238 in 1953), migration histories and chief genealogies.

The Mbe verb: A description of the verb system of Mbe, a language of Northern Cross River State, Nigeria (unpublished)' — i.e. the Ekoid Mbe [mfo] of Nigeria, not this Cameroonian language; the PHOIBLE assignment to mbee1250 is a misidentification.
